title: One rook crosses the boards five times, then mates
summary: On board A White attacked from the opening and stayed ahead; on board B White pressed first, then Black counterattacked with pawns and pieces fed from board A, and after the score swung both ways Black was mating there at the end. Follow the rook that started on h1 of board B: it crosses between the boards five times, and its last trip, Qxh8 on board B, gives White on board A R@d8#.
event: HypeBeast 1.1.1 against itself, 500,000 nodes a move for one team and 450,000 for the other

result.text: White on board A mates; the team of A-White and B-Black wins.

moves.note: Its first choice was Be7. It took the rook on h3 with check instead, expecting a pawn to come over from board A, which came at once (gxf7). The rook went to White on board A, who dropped it with check on f7, R@f7+. This rook started on h1 of board B, and it will cross the boards four more times.
The rook from board B takes Black's queen with check. The queen goes to Black on board B, who drops it on c8 (Q@c8), and after Nxe7 the rook goes back to White on board B, who drops it on h4 (R@h4).

White took the h5 pawn en passant instead of its first choice, P@g2. If nothing came across, the two scored nearly the same, but the engine thought it more likely than not that Black here would get a knight from board A, and with a knight in Black's hand it scored P@g2 almost four pawns worse than the capture. The knight came at once, from Bxh5 on board A, and Black dropped it on d4.

lines.note: Black's answer in a fresh search: Be7, with White still about three pawns ahead by the engine's count.
Its first choice, P@g2, the move it scored best if nothing arrived.
With the knight in Black's hand: N@d4 at once, which was Black's actual reply in the game.

moves.note: Black dropped a pawn on g2 with check and by its own count was winning by a wide margin if nothing came from board B. It gave about one chance in four that White would get a rook, and in that case already scored the drop as losing. The rook came at once, from Bxh4 on board B. After Kxg2 White's search had White well ahead, with Q@g4 to block the queen check, and the game went that way. The pawn taken on g2 went to Black on board B, who dropped it with check: P@g3+.

lines.note: Black's own expectation: after Kxg2, another pawn drop on g4.
White's line at its next turn: block Q@g5+ with Q@g4, and after P@f3+ Kxf3 White is about eight pawns ahead by its count.

moves.note: Black takes White's rook on h4 with the bishop, and the rook crosses back to White on board A, just after Black there played P@g2+. Black here also expected a pawn from board A, and Kxg2 sent it the pawn just dropped on g2. After gxh4 the bishop goes to Black on board A.

This is the pawn Black on board A dropped on g2: Kxg2 sent it here. Its first choice was N@f1+, but the engine expected another pawn to come over from board A, and in that case it scored the pawn check well ahead of the knight check. Another pawn did come, from Kxf3, and Black dropped it with check two moves later, P@f3+.

lines.note: White's answer in a fresh search: Kxg3 and the knight check N@h5+, with Black about six pawns ahead.
Its first choice, the knight check N@f1+, which it played a move later anyway.
A search that ignores the other board plays R@g6; searched the same way, it scored much lower than the pawn check.
Its plan had the second pawn already been in hand: P@f4.

moves.note: Its first choice was Qxf4. It dropped the rook with check instead, because by its count the check did better if a pawn or a knight came from board B, which it thought likely. A knight came at once, from fxe2+.

Its first choice was Bxe8, but a deeper search of the same position changed it to Rxe8. The captured rook goes to White on board B, who drops it on h8 (R@h8). Black's queen takes it there at the end and sends it back to board A for the mate.

Its first choice was N@f2. It dropped the pawn instead because, if Black received a pawn from board A, it scored the knight drop much worse. But Black had just received a bishop from Qxf7 on board A, and B@h3+ followed at once. At its next turn White's score was over forty pawns down. Nothing here shows whether N@f2 would have held.

lines.note: Black's answer in a fresh search: B@h3+, with Black about fourteen pawns ahead.
Its first choice, N@f2, which its own search scored slightly in White's favour.
Black's line at its next turn: B@h3+ and knight checks; most of its large score is what its captures would hand its partner on board A.

moves.note: The bishop came from board A, where White took it with Qxf7 a move earlier. By the engine's count any one piece Black captured here was enough for its partner on board A to mate, so its line is a run of checks that captures on e2 and g1, and its whole score comes from the value of those captures on board A: counting this board alone, the same line left Black about four pawns worse.

lines.note: A search that ignores the other board plays Ke7 instead, and it scored well below B@h3+ when both were searched the same way.
A search with four times the nodes preferred Rxf2+ first; searched the same way it scored worse than B@h3+, and the game reached Rxf2+ a move later anyway.
White's actual reply, P@g2, and Black's line at its next turn, which the game followed as far as Kf1.

moves.note: White blocked the check with a pawn on g2; a knight there scored the same, and both were lost by its count. It counted any piece it lost on this board as enough for White on board A to mate, so more than half of its very bad score is what its losses would hand over there.

lines.note: The game followed this line for four moves, then Black chose N@d2+ instead of R@h1+.

moves.note: White took the knight on e7 with check. That knight went to its partner on board B, who dropped it with check, N@d2+, a few moves later, and Black's king here had a single move, Kc8. White's search had it about sixteen pawns up.

lines.note: White's expected continuation: Kc8, then a queen takes the bishop on f4.
Black's own line at its next turn agrees, and still has White about eight pawns ahead.

moves.note: Black sat in check for half a second before its only move. After Kc8 a rook on d8 would mate, and on board B Black's queen on e8 could take White's rook on h8 with Qxh8, sending exactly that piece to White here. While Black sits, White cannot move on this board, so no rook can be dropped.

lines.note: Black expected White to take the bishop on f4, and White did, with the other queen.

moves.note: White took the bishop on f4, which went to its partner on board B. Taking with the g4 queen scored nearly the same by its count, and a little better in a search that ignores the other board. It made no difference: the rook for R@d8# reached White's hand from board B before its next move.

lines.note: White's expected line; the game ended before any of it was played.
A search that ignores the other board takes with the other queen, and scored it a little higher than the move played.

moves.note: Black sat again for 0.6 seconds, for the same reason: Black's queen on board B could still take the rook on h8, and a rook on d8 would mate here. Then it took the bishop on h5, which went to White on board B. By its own count Black was about six pawns down. As soon as it moved, Black on board B played Qxh8 and White dropped the rook on d8 for mate.

lines.note: Black's expected line, never played: the mate came from board B first.
What White would play with a free move instead of Black's sit: P@f7, with White about fifteen pawns ahead by the engine's count.

moves.note: Its first choice was N4f3+, a mate in three on this board by its count. It took the rook on h8 instead, because that rook goes straight to its partner on board A, where a rook on d8 mates at once. White on board A was already sitting, waiting for it. This is the rook that started on h1 of this board, and its fifth trip across the boards ends the game.

lines.note: The engine's answer for White here, gxh8=Q+, was never played: the game ended on board A first.
Its first choice: a mate in three on this board, slower than the mate on board A.

moves.note: White sat for just over a second because its partner on board B, on turn, could take a piece that gave it a winning drop. Black's queen took the rook on h8, the rook arrived, and R@d8# ended the game. Black on board A had twice sat to hold this off.
